blocks.text: The opening gives the woman a prominent, active voice: she expresses longing, praises her beloved, and describes herself as both dark and beautiful. Her words in verses 5–6 should not be read as making one description cancel the other; later translations and interpretations have sometimes treated them that way. The chapter also addresses the “daughters of Jerusalem” and includes other voices, but not every individual line can be assigned to a speaker with certainty.
The title calls this “the Song of songs” and associates it with Solomon. That association does not, by itself, unambiguously say that Solomon personally composed every lyric in the book.

Across the rest of the Song, recurring images, descriptions, searches, and phrases give the poems coherence, but they do not establish one uncontested storyline, wedding sequence, dream plot, or biography. Jewish and Christian readers have often read the lovers as representing God and Israel, or Christ and the church or soul; these are later theological readings rather than identifications made explicitly by the speakers. The Song is also preserved in four fragmentary Hebrew manuscripts from the Judean Desert and in a highly literal ancient Greek translation.

The Song’s voices, body praise, fragrances, and landscapes have substantial parallels in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian love poetry. Such parallels help place its poetic style alongside other ancient love poetry, without proving one direct source or a ritual setting. Its language is often read as compatible with later composition or shaping, while the surviving Qumran manuscripts show only that the Song already existed when those copies were made.
